newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo banks to clean-up, ready for IMF, creditors.
newsitem.headline: Yugo banks to clean-up, ready for IMF, creditors.

text.p: Yugoslavia is gearing for a major clean-up of its banking sector in the hope of a speedy resumption of talks with world financial institutions.
But western analysts expressed scepticism over the government's commitment to reform the sector, saying its efforts were just a cosmetic change and did not address the problem at its root.

"It looks like the government is set to revive the banking sector by increasing its control over it. But that has hardly ever given results elsewhere in the world," a London-based investment banker told Reuters on Wednesday.
A U.S. economist said a clean-up and revival of the banking sector was desirable but feared the government was assuming too much control over scarce finances.

"Yugoslav banking system already looks very centralised and messy. Investors would not necessarily look at (bank clean-up) adversly. But they would certainly not approve of further centralisation," the economist said.
The announced bank overhaul programme is planned to clear banks' balances from external commercial debt, claims and frozen savings, amounting to around eight billion dollars.

The country's largest banking group, Beogradska Banka, announced early in April its own independent rehabilitation programme with the setting up of a special agency to take over debt from its member banks.

The move by Beogradska, which has 20 members, came two weeks after Borka Vucic, a close associate of Serbia's president Slobodan Milosevic and until recently head of the bank's Cyprus affiliate, returned to Belgrade to take over as general manager.
Vucic said the agency will first register all debts and claims of its member banks and later offer them for sale on the market.

"Our own bank rehabilitation agency should be an institution which will let us know where we stand. When we clear banks from external debt, our banks' balances will become cleaner and healthier," she added.

But a western banker who asked not to be named said: "It is one thing to clean-up the books, but they do not offer a real solution to the problem. And another issue is how to attract fresh funds to the system."
Yugoslavia's external debt is unofficially estimated at around nine billion dollars, but there are no official figures.
The country has been banned from access to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), World Bank and world capital markets since U.N. sanctions were imposed in 1992.
Although sanctions were formally lifted in October 1996, Yugoslavia remained under the so-called outer wall of sanctions keeping it away from the IMF and desperately needed foreign cash.

To regain access to foreign funds, Belgrade has to cooperate with the Hague War Crimes Tribunal, improve its human rights record in its majority-Albanian southern province of Kosovo and speed up negotiations with other republics of the former Balkan federation on division of assets.

From the bankers point of view, sorting out liabilities in the banks' balances and making a clear register of commercial and government debt was seen as a precondition for Yugoslavia to begin talks with the IMF and its creditors.
"Bank rehabilitation is a big preparation for the IMF arrival in Yugoslavia and we must prepare to work with the IMF," Vucic said.
Coming to terms with international financial community may also help Yugoslavia collect sizeable claims from its debtors, she said.
